{"id": "89:11/q02", "question": "How is 'those who transgressed' parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether the relative expression remains a modifier without ellipsis or is detached as censure, and, if detached, whether its implied construction is accusative or nominative.", "positions": [{"id": "89:11/q02/p1", "position": "It is accusative as an expression of censure or blame, with an implied verb such as 'I mean.'", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī call this the best parse; al-Qurṭubī prefers it. Al-Bursawī reports al-Zamakhsharī's view that this implied reproach better suits the meaning. Al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Ālūsī, and Bint al-Shāṭiʾ record it as possible; al-Ālūsī says the same parsing carries into 89:12. Al-Ālūsī's full text says the detached censure can mean each tyrant."}, {"id": "89:11/q02/p2", "position": "It is genitive, a modifier of the previously named ʿĀd, Thamūd, and Pharaoh.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī prefers this because it requires no ellipsis, although he acknowledges the force of the accusative reproach. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says all three parses are formally valid but rhetorically unequal and favors this connected modifier. Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn, and al-Ālūsī also allow the construction; al-Ālūsī extends the parallel parsing to 89:12."}, {"id": "89:11/q02/p3", "position": "It is nominative after an omitted subject, 'they are,' as a separate statement of blame.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Ālūsī, and Bint al-Shāṭiʾ give this as a possible parse; al-Ālūsī applies the parallel analysis to 89:12. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ accepts its formal validity but prefers the connected modifier."}]}
{"id": "89:11/q03", "question": "What does 'they transgressed' mean here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "89:11/q03/p1", "position": "They overstepped God's bounds through rebellious sin, disbelief, arrogance, injustice, and corruption, including oppression of prophets and other people.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Biqāʿī, and al-Nasafī give the basic sense as crossing limits; al-Ṭabarī specifies exceeding what God permitted and committing prohibited disbelief. Al-Jishumī compares corruption beyond its limit to water beyond its bank (69:11); Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says the water sense precedes the metaphor of tyrants' arrogance, and points to Moses' charge to Pharaoh (79:17). Corpus Coranicum refers the root ṭ-ġ-w/y to 96:6. Muqātil and al-Naḥḥās mention sins and defiance of God's command; al-Baghawī and his full text add arrogance. Al-Kalbī as reported by al-Ṭabrisī says they opposed prophets and spread killing and sin. Ibn al-Jawzī and al-Rāzī add tyranny over prophets, and al-Rāzī includes believers. Al-Qurṭubī says injustice and aggression; Ibn Kathīr says insolence, corruption, and harm to people. Al-Biqāʿī's full text specifies unbelief and injustice that others imitated. Almalılı says pride in strength and desire led to violations of justice and the rights of people and their Creator. Ibn ʿĀshūr and his full text call it extreme disobedience and injustice. Iṣlāḥī describes fearlessness toward God and the conceit that resources were self-earned and beyond accountability. Kur'an Yolu describes unrestrained rebellion and a country turned into sedition and corruption through disregard of guidance and justice. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī and Study Quran couple tyranny with spreading corruption."}]}
{"id": "89:11/q04", "question": "Which lands does 'in the lands' cover?", "turns_on": "Whether the plural is limited distributively to each people's own country or also encompasses territory within their potential coercive reach.", "positions": [{"id": "89:11/q04/p1", "position": "Each people transgressed in its own land; the plural distributes the act among their respective territories.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī calls them their lands, and al-Naḥḥās says they lived there. Al-Bursawī assigns ʿĀd to Yemen, Thamūd to Syria, Egyptians to Egypt, and Nimrod to Sawād. Al-Ālūsī says each tyrant transgressed in his own land. Ibn ʿĀshūr and his full text read the definite article as pointing to the already mentioned peoples' lands, or as contextually restricted to them, and take the plural distributively; he adds that local oppression spreads through the lands."}, {"id": "89:11/q04/p2", "position": "Their transgression reached the lands they ruled and those they could dominate by force.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī expressly includes both actual rule and potential coercive reach; his full text says Pharaoh, his army, ʿĀd, Thamūd, and their followers exceeded limits in the lands they ruled."}]}
{"id": "89:11/q05", "question": "What effects does tyranny have on a society?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "89:11/q05/p1", "position": "It spreads corruption by damaging rulers, the oppressed, shared values, social bonds, and the ability to resist harm.", "reasons": "Sayyid Quṭb says the tyrant becomes enslaved to desire and claims God's place, as Pharaoh did (79:24); the oppressed lose dignity, creativity, and ambition while resentment and degraded desires grow; rulers falsify values because sound standards threaten their power. Ibn ʿĀshūr says tyranny teaches rights violations, breeds hatred and fear, divides society, and weakens resistance to external enemies; oppression beginning locally spreads through the lands. Al-Biqāʿī's full text says unbelief and injustice become imitated precedents."}]}
{"id": "89:11/q06", "question": "What lesson do the transgressors' histories teach about God's response?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "89:11/q06/p1", "position": "God watches powerful, corrupt nations, grants them time, then punishes persistent rebellion; their strength cannot prevent judgment, which also warns individuals of accountability.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says the cited ʿĀd, Iram, Thamūd, and Pharaoh carry this core lesson: transgression and corruption met punishment under God's watch. She says exegetes disagree widely about additional historical details and further sin catalogues are unnecessary. Iṣlāḥī says God controls persons and nations, sets their respite, permits reform or a final communication of truth, then seizes those still rebellious even at their zenith; the destruction anticipates each person's full reward or punishment. Kur'an Yolu says material strength cannot avert punishment for denial and rebellion, and the warning extends to rulers and other responsible people who abandon guidance and justice. It says the first audience likely knew the stories by report or ruins, and knew the peoples for strength and corruption."}]}
{"id": "89:11/q07", "question": "How do these historical examples relate to the surah's oath answer?", "turns_on": "Whether the historical lessons themselves evidence an omitted oath answer or prepare for the answer stated later.", "positions": [{"id": "89:11/q07/p1", "position": "They supply evidence for an unspoken answer to the opening oaths.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr's full text gives this as one way the historical lessons function in the surah."}, {"id": "89:11/q07/p2", "position": "They delay the stated answer, 'Your Lord is indeed watching,' building suspense and preparing the audience for it.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr's full text gives this as the alternative relation of the examples to the later answer."}]}
{"id": "89:11/q08", "question": "What earlier poetic parallel is noted for the catalogue of punished peoples?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "89:11/q08/p1", "position": "A verse attributed to the early poet Zuhayr lists Pharaoh among people God destroyed and resembles Qur'anic catalogues of punishment.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum notes that Zuhayr names individuals where the Qur'anic catalogue names collectives, and suggests the Qur'anic historical cycles may develop related ideas."}]}
{"id": "89:11/q09", "question": "How is the nearby 'bi-l-wādī' read?", "turns_on": "Whether the yāʾ is retained or omitted in connected reading and at a pause.", "positions": [{"id": "89:11/q09/p1", "position": "The final yāʾ is retained both in connected reading and at a pause.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī reports this for al-Qawwās, al-Bazzī, and Yaʿqūb."}, {"id": "89:11/q09/p2", "position": "The final yāʾ is retained in connected reading and dropped at a pause.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī reports this for Warsh."}, {"id": "89:11/q09/p3", "position": "The final yāʾ is omitted both in connected reading and at a pause.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī attributes this to the other readers."}]}
{"id": "89:11/q10", "question": "How is the subsequent 'scourge' described?", "turns_on": "Whether the scourge is explained as the specific whip or as the punishment it signifies.", "positions": [{"id": "89:11/q10/p1", "position": "It is a kind of punishment poured upon the transgressors.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī reports Qatāda's gloss of the scourge in the ensuing punishment verse."}, {"id": "89:11/q10/p2", "position": "It is the familiar whip, perhaps so named because its strike mixes flesh.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn gives this lexical explanation alongside his parsing of 'those who transgressed.'"}]}

{"id": "89:15/q02", "question": "What work does ammā do?", "turns_on": "Paired contrast and conditional linkage are the two emphases.", "positions": [{"id": "89:15/q02/p1", "position": "Its conditional force calls for the fāʾ in the predicate.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī and al-Ālūsī explain the fāʾ; al-Biqāʿī says the time phrase emphasizes the onset of trial."}, {"id": "89:15/q02/p2", "position": "It sets up a paired contrast of prosperity and restriction and strengthens each response's link to the discourse.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says ammā has a 'whatever may happen' force, normally pairs contrasts rather than unpacks a summary, and compares 2:26."}]}
{"id": "89:15/q03", "question": "Who is al-insān?", "turns_on": "Generic humanity, unbelievers as a class, or named individuals.", "positions": [{"id": "89:15/q03/p1", "position": "Umayya ibn Khalaf.", "reasons": "Muqātil and several transmitters identify him; Ibn ʿĀshūr also attributes this to al-Kalbī."}, {"id": "89:15/q03/p2", "position": "An unbeliever or Meccan polytheist who denies resurrection.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj, al-Wāḥidī, al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī and Ibn ʿĀshūr associate the outlook with denied recompense; Quraysh treated wealth and children as rank."}, {"id": "89:15/q03/p3", "position": "The human type, including some believers who think this way.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān say Muslims can share the mistake; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ says generic does not mean every person. Ibn ʿĀshūr says polytheists predominate in the audience."}, {"id": "89:15/q03/p4", "position": "Ubayy ibn Khalaf.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbī or Ibn al-Sāʾib is cited; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ jointly cites al-Kalbī and Muqātil."}, {"id": "89:15/q03/p5", "position": "ʿUtba ibn Rabīʿa and Abū Ḥudhayfa ibn al-Mughīra.", "reasons": "The pair is attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, sometimes through ʿAṭāʾ; Ibn ʿĀshūr gives their names as alternatives. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ varies ʿUtba's name."}, {"id": "89:15/q03/p6", "position": "ʿUtba ibn Rabīʿa alone.", "reasons": "Al-Suhaylī names him while allowing general application; Ibn ʿĀshūr lists him individually."}, {"id": "89:15/q03/p7", "position": "Abū Ḥudhayfa ibn al-Mughīra alone.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr lists him as the other alternative."}]}
{"id": "89:15/q04", "question": "How do the time and saying clauses parse?", "turns_on": "Which clause predicates the subject and what governs the fronted time phrase.", "positions": [{"id": "89:15/q04/p1", "position": "Fa-yaqūlu predicates al-insān, idhā modifies it despite being fronted, and the second clause has an implicit subject.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī support this; al-Shihāb calls it correct. Abū Ḥayyān says the fāʾ does not bar the temporal attachment."}, {"id": "89:15/q04/p2", "position": "Idhā is a condition, yaqūlu its answer, and the whole condition predicates al-insān.", "reasons": "Abū al-Baqāʾ is reported by al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī. Al-Samīn objects that ammā's required fāʾ is lost except after omitted speech or in necessity; he cites 3:106."}, {"id": "89:15/q04/p3", "position": "The time phrase belongs to an implied 'state of the human'.", "reasons": "Al-Jalabī proposes this after claiming consensus against the ordinary parse; al-Ālūsī says its saying predicate becomes strained."}, {"id": "89:15/q04/p4", "position": "A phrase can precede the fāʾ only if it is the sole separator after ammā.", "reasons": "Al-Raḍī, al-Damāmīnī and followers disallow an additional separator."}]}

{"id": "89:15/q06", "question": "What does ibtalāhu mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "89:15/q06/p1", "position": "God tested or tried him, including by a favorable gift.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Qurṭubī and Ibn ʿĀshūr use 'test'; al-Sāmarrāʾī says ابتلى is stronger than بلا and balāʾ need not be harmful. Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 21:35 and 27:40."}]}
{"id": "89:15/q07", "question": "What is accomplished by testing through fortune?", "turns_on": "Moral trial, manifestation of known character, or wise governance.", "positions": [{"id": "89:15/q07/p1", "position": "Abundance tests gratitude and generosity, while restriction tests patience and contentment.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī, al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān and Ibn ʿĀshūr cite 21:35; Ibn ʿĀshūr adds 27:40. Qāshānī invokes faith's halves of patience and gratitude. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ and Iṣlāḥī add others' rights and 89:28."}, {"id": "89:15/q07/p2", "position": "It brings out known good or evil and establishes proof and accountability.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī lists competing calls of reason, law, guidance and Satan; al-Burhān says righteous and wicked are tested to establish proof; Elmalılı connects duties with reckoning."}, {"id": "89:15/q07/p3", "position": "Allotments follow God's wisdom, welfare and varied causes, not an observable simple rule.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī stresses wisdom; Ibn ʿĀshūr describes ordinary and extraordinary causes, repeated tests (9:126), and the need for caution about hidden intentions."}]}
{"id": "89:15/q08", "question": "Why is there a fāʾ before 'honored him'?", "turns_on": "Explanatory identity versus causal sequence.", "positions": [{"id": "89:15/q08/p1", "position": "It explains what the prosperous test consists of; honor and ease are one combined gift.", "reasons": "Abū al-Suʿūd and al-Ālūsī take the fāʾ as explanatory; al-Ālūsī says the human compresses the two gifts into one statement."}, {"id": "89:15/q08/p2", "position": "It is causal: honor and blessing flow through a test with duties.", "reasons": "Elmalılı rejects the explanatory analysis and distinguishes grant from trial."}]}
{"id": "89:15/q09", "question": "What does 'He honored him' mean here?", "turns_on": "Worldly benefit versus proof of approved rank.", "positions": [{"id": "89:15/q09/p1", "position": "He received money, status, social respect, or another worldly good.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī's specialists distinguish this from the opposite of humiliation; al-Biqāʿī mentions social esteem. Al-Rāzī notes that God calls the first state honor but never calls poverty humiliation. Ibn ʿĀshūr says informed theologians agree unbelievers receive worldly blessings."}]}

Elmalılı distinguishes increased provision from status; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it a state of comfort."}]}
{"id": "89:15/q11", "question": "Why pair comfort with restricted provision instead of pairing honor with humiliation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "89:15/q11/p1", "position": "Withholding a gift is not an insult and poor righteous people are not disgraced.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī compares a patron who neither gives nor insults. Ibn ʿĀshūr says this audience generally retained bodily health and cites al-Nābigha about death by killing or age."}, {"id": "89:15/q11/p2", "position": "The first clause names an actual gift, while the second only names reduced provision.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī and Qatāda observe the text affirms honor in the first case but not humiliation in the second."}]}
{"id": "89:15/q12", "question": "How is the human's speech presented?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "89:15/q12/p1", "position": "As a recurring, literal and confident boast, often without gratitude.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī notes joy without thanks; al-Biqāʿī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ note pride. {"id": "89:15/q13", "question": "How is the yāʾ in rabbī read?", "turns_on": "Fatḥa or sukūn on the possessive yāʾ.", "positions": [{"id": "89:15/q13/p1", "position": "With fatḥa.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī cites Ḥijāz and Abū ʿAmr; al-Jishumī adds Abū Jaʿfar, Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr and Yaʿqūb; Ibn ʿĀshūr names Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr. {"id": "89:15/q15", "question": "What does the human imply by 'my Lord honored me'?", "turns_on": "Self-meriting approval versus acknowledgment of a limited gift.", "positions": [{"id": "89:15/q15/p1", "position": "He assumes wealth proves deserved, lasting approval, entitlement or superiority.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Nasafī invoke Qārūn (28:78). Ibn ʿĀshūr cites Ṭarafa's boast and the chiefs demanding expulsion of poor believers (6:52); al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ says the person imagines license to act at will."}, {"id": "89:15/q15/p2", "position": "He recognizes a real benefit, which alone does not reveal divine approval.", "reasons": "Qatāda allows the limited claim; al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī and Ibn ʿĀshūr distinguish receiving a gift from having approved rank."}]}
{"id": "89:15/q16", "question": "What is real honor or disgrace?", "turns_on": "Obedience, afterlife result, or unknowable worldly purpose.", "positions": [{"id": "89:15/q16/p1", "position": "Honor follows obedience, piety, faith and good action; disgrace follows sin or abandonment.", "reasons": "Mujāhid, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Baghawī and others make the contrast. Al-Nasafī calls honor enablement to obey. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ reports al-Ṭabarī's preference; the Study Quran cites a ḥadīth qudsī and 49:13."}, {"id": "89:15/q16/p2", "position": "Final standing is known in the Hereafter, not from present fortune.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī argues pleasure ending in damnation is no honor and hardship ending in salvation no disgrace; wealth can impede worship and make death painful. He says this reasoning presupposes resurrection, yet even without it wealth may invite murder or robbery and lack may preserve safety. Al-Jishumī locates recompense at resurrection."}, {"id": "89:15/q16/p3", "position": "No automatic worldly sign is reliable because God's purposes and causes differ.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 6:44, 7:94–95 and 9:126 for testing and punishment, yet 16:97, 71:10–12 and 72:16 for temporal reward; extraordinary victories can signal special treatment. Al-Nābigha counsels awareness of changing outcomes and Ibn al-Rāwandī's couplet observes reversed fortunes."}]}
